processing: A layered drink poured in one glass: teas and flavoured liquids of different densities settle in visibly separate bands. The exact recipe is kept secret by its maker.
harvest_season: Not tied to a harvest; made to order with local tea all year.
appearance_dry: Not sold as dry leaf; the base teas are local Bangladeshi teas in unspecified combinations.
appearance_liquor: Distinct horizontal bands from pale cream through amber to dark reddish brown in a tall glass.
appearance_wet: No leaf is visible in the glass, which holds only the layered liquids.
taste_profile: Tasters report sweet, spiced layers with cinnamon, lemon, cloves and condensed milk, changing as you drink down the glass.

brewing.notes: Not a home brew in any strict sense; the recipe is secret, and these numbers only suggest a strong base. Pour very slowly over a spoon if you experiment, heaviest liquids first.

vintage_note: Sold by the glass, not the packet. There are no years or seasons. The drink is made and drunk on the spot, mainly in Sreemangal, and copies with varying layer counts are found across Bangladesh.
description:
Saat rong cha is the layered tea of Sreemangal in Bangladesh's tea country, a tall glass with stacked bands of colour. It is more a piece of tea-stall showmanship than a type of leaf.

The trick relies on liquids of different densities settling over each other rather than mixing. The maker credited with it keeps the details private, so what goes in each layer is only known in part; tasters pick out cinnamon, lemon, cloves and condensed milk.

Sip it slowly and the layers come through as a run of sweet and spiced tastes rather than one tea flavour.

The place to try it is Sreemangal, at the Nilkantha Tea Cabin or one of its neighbours. Imitations are widespread, and the number of layers varies, so ask what you are ordering. It is a treat for curiosity, not for studying leaf.
history:
The drink is credited to Romesh Ram Gour (also spelled Ramesh Ram Gaur), a tea vendor in Sreemangal who is said to have worked it out from the differing densities of teas. He serves it at Nilkantha Tea Cabin. The start date is uncertain: one press account gives 2002, and Arab News dates his shop to 2006.

The story is not entirely tidy. Arab News reported that Gour developed a five-layer tea and that a neighbouring vendor, Saiful Islam, was inspired by it to make his own seven-colour version.
